hero.bandTitle: Good care starts with trust and understanding

namaste.title: Care that listens first.
body: After more than a decade in geriatric medicine in Nepal, I have sat with farmers, grandparents, teachers and their families as several small problems stacked into a life that suddenly felt unsafe. A fall, a new tablet, poor sleep, a change in memory. Each of them deserves the same thing: time, an honest explanation, and a plan written in words they understand.

journey.title: Your health journey
journey.lede: Good geriatric care is a sequence, not a single visit. These are the steps I keep joined up in clinic, in teaching and in national programmes.

steps.title: Understand the person
steps.text: Health, daily activities, relationships and what matters most, before any test or tablet.

steps.title: Screen and assess
steps.text: Frailty, falls, memory, medicines and nutrition, using tools that can work in Nepal.

steps.title: Plan together
steps.text: A written plan families can follow, with benefits and burdens spoken aloud.

steps.title: Support families
steps.text: Caregivers are partners. They need skills, information and care for themselves too.

steps.title: Keep care going
steps.text: Referral, rehabilitation and follow-up so a screening result does not become a dead end.

why.title: Ageing well is not a luxury.
body: The WHO Integrated Care for Older People pathway starts where families already are: with a health worker asking what an older person can still do, not only what they have been diagnosed with. Screen for loss of capacity, agree a plan, refer where needed, keep following up.

ICOPE is now being built into services in Nepal, and that is the work I know best. In a country where several manageable problems can stack into a crisis, healthy ageing is a service question. It needs trained people, simple tools and a plan a family can hold.
why.quote: Growing up in Nepal and watching older family members taught me that dignity, support and the right care are not extras. They are the work.

hero.title: Dr. Ramesh Kandel.
lede: A physician specialising in geriatric medicine, working across clinical practice, research, medical education and institutional leadership in Nepal.

lead.kicker: Stop the guesswork and finally get answers
lead.title: Have you ever asked yourself
questions: Is this **normal ageing**, or is something actually wrong?
Are all of these **medicines** still needed, and for how long?
What do we do after a **fall**, before the next one happens?
Is this **memory change** treatable, or something the family simply accepts?
Who do we call when **every specialist** says something different?
What will the **next ten years** look like, honestly?

body: **I am a physician specialising in geriatric medicine**, working across clinical practice, research, medical education and institutional leadership in Nepal.

**My training began at B.P. Koirala Institute of Health Sciences** and continued in Geriatric Medicine at the All India Institute of Medical Sciences, New Delhi. That training shaped how I care for older adults: looking beyond individual diagnoses to understand how illness affects independence, wellbeing and everyday life.

**My interest in older people’s health has personal roots.** Growing up in Nepal and observing the experiences of older family members helped me recognise the importance of dignity, support and access to appropriate care.

**Much of my work now builds the services around the person.** At Rapti Academy of Health Sciences that has included academic leadership as Dean of the School of Medicine, hospital administration as Hospital Director and Medical Director, and the development of medicine and geriatric services. Before that I led geriatric services at the Hospital for Advanced Medicine and Surgery, taught at Patan Academy of Health Sciences, and worked as a consultant on healthy ageing at the WHO South-East Asia Regional Office in New Delhi.
Several manageable problems can combine into a crisis: a fall, a new medicine, poor nutrition, a change in memory that reaches the whole family.

Good care means careful listening, sound judgement and decisions made with the person rather than around them. The same principle guides my research and teaching: work that responds to real needs and can be delivered in local settings.

hero.title: Grounded in clinical and community needs.
lede: My research focuses on improving care for older adults and people living with chronic conditions. I look for approaches that are practical, affordable and responsive to patients, caregivers and health professionals in Nepal.

lead.kicker: Questions that start in the clinic
lead.title: What the work keeps asking
questions: How do **several conditions together** change independence, risk and what care should actually do?
Can **community screening** lead to assessment, a plan, referral and follow-up?
What supports people and families **between visits**, not only in hospital?
How do people carry the **mental load** of long-term disease, and what helps?
After a fall or a medicine change, which **results matter** to older people?
How does evidence become **routine practice**, and what does it cost?

body: **My research begins in the clinic and the community.** It focuses on improving care for older adults and people living with chronic conditions, looking for approaches that are practical, affordable and responsive to patients, caregivers and health professionals in Nepal.

**Integrated Care for Older People is a central thread.** My work explores how the WHO ICOPE approach can be adapted to local services and communities: identifying implementation needs, supporting health-worker training and examining how screening can lead to assessment, care planning, referral and follow-up.

**I served as programme coordinator and consultant** for the WHO-supported project developing an ICOPE implementation model in Lumbini Province, and as a member of the WHO Clinical Consortium on Healthy Ageing in Geneva.

**My clinical research interests include frailty, falls and other geriatric syndromes**, alongside antimicrobial resistance in older patients. These areas reflect challenges encountered in routine practice and the need for evidence that can inform care in Nepal.
Adapting WHO guidance to Nepali services, so screening becomes assessment, a plan and follow-up rather than a form.
Studying frailty, geriatric syndromes and antimicrobial resistance where they actually occur, in routine practice and local settings.
statement.note: Research that stays on a shelf changes nothing. The test is whether a district health worker or a family at home can use it.

hero.title: Healthy ageing is a service question.
lede: Nepal is ageing faster than the health services around it were designed for. The WHO Integrated Care for Older People pathway is the practical answer I work with, in clinic, in district programmes and in the classroom.

lead.kicker: What the pathway has to survive
lead.title: The questions behind the programme
questions: Can a community health worker assess **intrinsic capacity** with tools that need no laboratory?
What follows a **positive screen**: a plan and a referral, or a dead end?
Who **follows up** when the person is at home and the nearest clinic is a day away?
How do **families** become partners rather than bystanders?
What changes when **one trained person** joins a district hospital team?
How does **national guidance** reach a ward that is short of everything?

body: **I served as programme coordinator and consultant** for the WHO-supported project developing an ICOPE implementation model in Lumbini Province: identifying what the services needed, training health workers, and testing how screening can lead to assessment, a care plan, referral and follow-up.

**Healthy ageing is not a service of its own.** It is ordinary care, organised so that capacity is measured early, medicines are reviewed, falls are taken seriously and someone keeps in touch. Most of that belongs to primary care, where Nepali older people already go.

**In 2019 I worked as Consultant on Healthy Ageing for WHO-SEARO** in New Delhi, and I am a member of the WHO Clinical Consortium on Healthy Ageing in Geneva. Both roles keep the Nepali work in conversation with guidance written for settings like it.
**The part I would defend longest** is follow-up. A screening result without a plan, or a plan without a phone call, teaches families that the system asks questions but does not answer them.
Geriatric services staffed, sized and measured like any other specialty, from the district hospital outward to the community.
Screening that leads somewhere: a written plan a family can follow, and someone who checks whether it worked.

help.title: Your health is not a destination, it’s a journey.
body: Although you may be currently struggling with an illness or symptoms, my focus is on restoring function and independence rather than just treating disease. This approach may be different from what you are used to, but it is far superior for improving your overall quality of life and reducing your future risk of dependence.
I only work with people who are ready to make changes and who I know I can help. If I do not think that I can help you I will refer you to someone or something that can.
To determine if this type of consultation is a good fit for you, click the button below and send a short enquiry. I will be in touch shortly with details.
help.note: Send an enquiry and I will reply with availability, directions and what to bring.

first.title: Build your health story and gain clarity about the years ahead.
body: Before the first appointment, write the story in your own words: the medical history, the current challenges, and the goals that matter most to you and your family.

left.title: Memory and thinking
left.text: A simple bedside screening of recall, attention and language, explained as we go.

right.title: Mood and motivation
right.text: A screening for low mood, anxiety, apathy and the losses that accompany them.

left.title: Function and gait
left.text: How you rise, walk, turn and sit, observed and timed at your own pace.

right.title: Falls and balance
right.text: A determination of your level of fall risk and the confidence lost after a fall.

left.title: Medicines and prescriptions
left.text: Every tablet, injection and remedy matched against its purpose, benefit and burden.

right.title: Nutrition and weight
right.text: An assessment of appetite, weight, meals and the risk of deficiency.

left.title: Vision and hearing
left.text: A screening of the senses that quietly withdraw people from conversation and street life.

right.title: Sleep and continence
right.text: A review of nights, daytime tiredness and the problems people rarely volunteer.

left.title: Heart, lungs and circulation
left.text: An examination of rate, rhythm, breath and the feet, with referral where needed.

right.title: Bones, joints and strength
right.text: A determination of arthritis, osteoporosis risk and the strength needed for daily life.

consult.title: One conversation, the whole picture.
body: During the first consultation we meet for a full hour, in person or by video, to prioritize your goals, review your history and medicines, determine the underlying causes of your complaints, and create a custom written plan.
consult.cardText: The first appointment is a full hour of focused time. I listen for the hidden details and ask the questions that reveal so much more than I can observe.

plan.title: A personalized written plan designed to protect your independence
body: Your custom plan will help to reduce your future risk of dependence, as well as the need for extra medicines and hospital visits.
Click below to see the areas that make up your complete plan.

items.title: Convenient
paragraphs: One appointment, one room, with the family present where possible, in person or by video.
Get all your important health questions answered without the usual barriers.

items.title: Time saving
paragraphs: There is no need to spend precious days moving from desk to desk to get a single answer.
The assessment, the review and the plan happen in one unhurried visit.

items.title: Get answers
paragraphs: Make more informed decisions about diet, fitness, and medicines based on your own health data.
Understand the steps that are needed to achieve your health goals.

track.title: Track your health progress over time.
body: From a **structured review of function, mood, medicines and falls** we will determine if the plan is working, if your exercise is adequate, and if every medicine is still worth its burden. In addition, monitoring these trends year after year helps us to determine if your health is declining, maintaining, or improving.

cta.title: Start to improve your
body: It is important to find and treat the root cause of decline, not just the symptoms. Let us work together to reverse your risk of dependence, reduce your reliance on prescription drugs, and optimize your health. Your custom plan will include low-risk, high-value recommendations in the areas of diet, lifestyle, fitness, and medicines so that you can start to live your healthiest life.

lede: Lectures, bedside teaching, skills workshops and curriculum work that prepare health professionals for an ageing population.

why.title: Lessons that travel across healthcare.
body: Geriatric medicine offers lessons every specialty needs: understanding several conditions at once, reviewing medicines thoughtfully, assessing function, and making decisions together with patients and families.
I teach the way I practise. A session starts with the person in front of us and ends with something the learner can repeat on their own ward.
Colleges, hospitals, professional bodies and community programmes are all welcome to ask for a session built around their own cases.
